title: After you're gone
hook: Honi meets a man planting a carob tree that won't fruit for seventy years
tomorrow: what did Thoreau say when asked to make his peace with God?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gerasim in the chair by the bed: presence, staying without the polite lie. Today, what's still here once there's no bed and no chair.

Carob tastes like chocolate that grew up on a farm: sweet, a little dusty, eaten straight from a long brown pod. The Talmud tells a story about a carob tree. Honi, a holy man known as the Circle-Drawer, is walking along a road and sees a man planting one. How long until it bears fruit? Honi asks. Seventy years, says the man. And you're sure you'll live seventy years? The man answers: I found the world full of carob trees. My ancestors planted them for me. So I'm planting these for my children.
screen: `SWEET, DUSTY, A BROWN POD.` → `A MAN PLANTING A CAROB.` → `SEVENTY YEARS TO FRUIT.` → `MY ANCESTORS PLANTED FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Then the story turns. Honi sits down to eat, sleep comes over him, a rock grows up around him, and he sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, a man is gathering carobs from that very tree. Did you plant this? Honi asks. No, says the man. I'm his grandson. The planter is gone. The fruit isn't. That's a Jewish teaching, and this path borrows it with its name on: you stand in a line, between the people who planted for you and the people you'll plant for. The rabbis push it further. A saying attributed to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai goes: if you're holding a sapling and someone shouts that the Messiah has come, plant the sapling first, then go out to greet him. The planting matters that much. So after you're gone isn't only a question about where you'll be. It's about what you're putting in the ground now: a tree, a recipe a kid will cook one day, a kindness someone learned by watching you. You won't taste most of it. It's still yours.
screen: `HONI SLEEPS SEVENTY YEARS.` · `THE GRANDSON GATHERS THE FRUIT.` · `A LINE: PLANTED FOR, PLANTING FOR.` · `PLANT THE SAPLING FIRST.` · then, large: `FOR AFTER.`

segments.voice: Hold something that grew: a seed, a leaf from a plant, a piece of fruit, or a pinch of soil. Feel its weight and its texture as you breathe. Then name, silently, one person who planted something you're still eating from, and one thing you might plant for after.
After you're gone: what you plant now that others will eat from later, the way Honi's planter fed a grandson he may never have met.
Carry this: for after, a tree whose fruit you may never taste. Six of seven, see you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1754 COUNTS.` → `AGING AND DEATH · 6 OF 7.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DID THOREAU SAY ABOUT MAKING PEACE WITH GOD?`
